To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Vietnamese firms involved in ordinary export activities are more productive and pay higher wages than firms that do not export.

Vietnamese exporters are highly heterogeneous, with more than half exporting more than 60% of their output, and that productivity and wage premia are positive only for ordinary exporters, and are higher for foreign owned than domestic firms.

Vietnamese exporters are heterogeneous in terms of their export regimes and firm ownership and that export premia are positive only for ordinary exporters and are higher for foreign owned than for domestic firms.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of firm heterogeneity in explaining the export patterns in a rapidly growing developing country and the role of firm ownership in explaining productivity and wage differences among Vietnamese exporters.
the following questions: (1) How do productivity and wages vary across firms in Vietnam that export ordinary products and those that export processed products?
the role of firm heterogeneity in explaining the export performance and productivity of Vietnamese firms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the export intensity distribution of Vietnamese exporters is more similar to that of other emerging economies than to the pattern observed in industrialized economies, but the wage and productivity patterns of Vietnamese exporters are closer to the latter group.
Vietnamese exporters, especially foreign owned ones, are not as productive as non exporters, which is in contrast to the pattern found in industrialized countries and other emerging economies.
the export premium is positive for Vietnamese ordinary exporters, but not for Vietnamese processing exporters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
while the export premium is positive and significant in Vietnam, the premium is only present for ordinary exporters.

the productivity and wage advantages that Vietnamese exporters enjoy relative to their non-exporters are concentrated among the group of exporters that are involved in ordinary trade, while exporters involved in processing trade do not exhibit such productivity and wage advantages.
while the export intensity distribution in Vietnam is similar to other emerging economies, export premia are positive only among ordinary exporters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the productivity gains from exporting are not uniform across all firms in Vietnam and are not as large as the gains from exporting in industrialized countries.

the export premia for processing firms in Vietnam are not only smaller but also negative, which implies that the export participation in the processing sector does not generate a positive impact on productivity and wage levels.
the productivity and wage premiums associated with exporting are not universal.
